articles.headline: OFAC Designates New Entities and Individuals in Latest Iran-Related Sanctions
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. This action is part of ongoing efforts to target individuals and entities supporting the Iranian regime.

Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities designated, and the reasons for their inclusion on the sanctions list, are expected to be elaborated in subsequent Treasury communications. These designations aim to disrupt illicit financial networks and activities that contribute to Iran's destabilizing behavior.

articles.headline: OFAC Expands Sanctions on Cuba's Military and Oil Sectors, Targets Cyber and Transnational Criminal Organizations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued new designations on November 5, 2026, targeting Cuba's military and oil sectors, alongside actions against cyber-related threats and transnational criminal organizations. This move expands the scope of U.S. sanctions against the Cuban regime and its supporting networks.

The sanctions include two individuals, five companies, and two ships linked to Cuba's military and oil sector. Among the sanctioned individuals is Brigadier General Any Lastres Morera, who leads GAESA, the powerful business conglomerate of the Cuban Armed Forces. State-owned companies Tecnosime, focused on natural gas and oil extraction, and Cubaelectronica, along with maritime transport firms Internacional Marítima and Petromarca, were also designated.

Additionally, OFAC expanded sanctions under Executive Order 14404 to cover the electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors of Cuba's economy, making foreign persons operating in these sectors potentially subject to U.S. sanctions. This action also included designations against four individuals and 41 entities supporting the Prince Group Transnational Criminal Organization, previously sanctioned for cyber-enabled fraud, money laundering, and human trafficking.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Demócrata / CP24 / CTV News / Customs & International Trade Law Firm

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran Sanctions, Updates Listings, Issues Alert on Shadow Fleet, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, alongside updates to existing Iran-related listings. These actions are part of the Trump administration's 'Operation Economic Outcast,' aimed at disrupting Iran's ability to fund its military and proxies through oil sales.

OFAC also published an Iran-related alert, specifically warning of the sanctions risk associated with dealing with potentially false-flagged vessels used by Iran's 'shadow fleet' for sanctions evasion. The U.S. State Department also announced sanctions targeting fraudulent ship registries and aviation support for the Iranian regime.

In a separate but related action, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a Frequently Asked Question. This amendment likely pertains to the ongoing easing of restrictions on Venezuela's oil, gas, and mining sectors, which have seen several general licenses issued since early 2026 following political changes in Venezuela.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / The Hindu / Daily Maverick / Customs & International Trade Law Firm / U.S. Department of State

body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026.

This amendment likely modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran, though specific details of the changes were not immediately available. Such amendments are often issued to clarify existing guidance or adjust the scope of permitted activities under the Iran sanctions program.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals in North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting entities and individuals related to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

For North Korea, the designations targeted 10 individuals and one entity for allegedly supporting government-run information technology (IT) worker schemes that defraud U.S. companies and generate revenue for North Korea's weapons and missile programs. These actions are part of a broader international effort to disrupt illicit revenue streams supporting the DPRK government.

Further details regarding the Democratic Republic of the Congo-related designations were not immediately available, but typically target individuals or entities involved in human rights abuses, corruption, or destabilizing activities in the region.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Reaches Settlement Agreement with OFAC
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc. on October 27, 2026.

The settlement resolves alleged violations of OFAC sanctions regulations. Extreme Networks, Inc. will pay $1,529,685 in civil penalties as part of this agreement. This action highlights OFAC's continued enforcement efforts to ensure compliance with U.S. sanctions laws.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking and Rejecting Transactions and Filing Reports
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026, regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC.

These amendments aim to provide updated guidance and clarity to financial institutions and other entities on their obligations under OFAC regulations. The FAQs are a crucial resource for ensuring compliance with U.S. sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Designations, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, and Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026. Simultaneously, OFAC removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea, indicating a recalibration of sanctions policy in these areas.

In addition to the designations and removals, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses, along with amended Frequently Asked Questions. These new general licenses and FAQs are expected to provide specific authorizations or clarifications for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the respective sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes PAIPA Designations on Chinese Entities, Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026, targeting Chinese entities.

These sanctions are in response to alleged theft of trade secrets, specifically related to Google's AI technology, marking the second-ever use of PAIPA and its first application against Chinese entities. The action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to combating intellectual property theft and protecting American innovation.

Alongside the designations, OFAC issued associated General Licenses to provide guidance and authorization for certain activities that might otherwise be prohibited. These licenses aim to mitigate unintended consequences while maintaining the effectiveness of the sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a Frequently Asked Question on October 16, 2026.

This amendment likely provides updated guidance or modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Venezuela. The U.S. has been issuing general licenses to ease restrictions on Venezuela's oil, gold, and mining sectors since early 2026, following significant political changes.
These ongoing adjustments reflect the evolving U.S. policy towards Venezuela, balancing sanctions pressure with efforts to facilitate humanitarian aid and support a democratic transition.

articles.headline: UK Sanctions List Corrects Entry for ZENITH GLOBAL CORPORATION LIMITED
body: On November 3, 2026, the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) updated the UK Sanctions List with a correction to the entry for ZENITH GLOBAL CORPORATION LIMITED (Unique ID: RUS3293).

The correction is an administrative amendment, with deleted information appearing in strikethrough and red, and newly added information underlined and highlighted in yellow. ZENITH GLOBAL CORPORATION LIMITED remains subject to asset freeze, trust services sanctions, director disqualification sanction, and transport sanctions.

Transport sanctions prohibit ships and aircraft owned, controlled, chartered, or operated by a designated person from entering or overflying the UK, and include prohibitions on technical assistance related to aircraft and ships.

articles.headline: China Expresses 'Serious Concern' Over US Sanctions Ahead of Xi-Trump Summit
body: China has expressed 'serious concern' over recent U.S. restrictions targeting the country, urging Washington to correct its 'wrongful practices as soon as possible.' This comes ahead of a planned meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump in Shenzhen.

The U.S. State Department announced sanctions on November 5 against China National Electronic Import and Export Company (CEIEC) and Beijing H&C Technologies, alleging their involvement in supplying military-related goods to Cuba through a Cuban arms procurement company. China's Ministry of Commerce firmly opposes these sanctions, stating they violate international law and harm Chinese companies' legitimate rights and interests.

The U.S. also recently extended the suspension of its 'Affiliates Rule' until January 10, 2027, a move seen by analysts as reflecting the Trump administration's reluctance to implement extreme measures against China before the summit. This rule would extend U.S. export restrictions to any company at least 50% owned by firms on the U.S. Entity List or Military End-User List.
articles.source: South China Morning Post / Syrian Arab News Agency

articles.headline: BIS Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors, Transfers to EAR
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List.

This deregulatory action aims to align export controls on suppressors with those already applied to firearms, reducing the compliance burden on the firearms industry while maintaining national security.

Under this new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and BIS will require a license for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers, including releases of related software and technology to foreign persons. License exceptions currently available for firearms will also be applicable to suppressors.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.
